stops.old: The 2022 Democratic Memory Law restored the name Cuelgamuros and plans its re-signification
stops.new: The Democratic Memory Law (Ley 20/2022) changed the official name from Valle de los Caídos to Valle de Cuelgamuros, made it a Place of Democratic Memory and plans its re-signification

stops.set: The monumental esplanade, the rock-cut basilica and the 150 m cross (the funicular up to the cross is closed indefinitely), with the Benedictine abbey behind.

stops.new: Paid entry; closed Mondays and some holidays. Opening days and prices change, so check the Patrimonio Nacional website just before you go.

stops.old: The painting toured to raise support for the Republic and then stayed in New York, as Picasso wished, until democracy returned to Spain; it arrived in Madrid in 1981 and moved to the Reina Sofía in 1992.
stops.new: The painting toured to raise support for the Republic. After the war it was looked after by the Museum of Modern Art in New York, which also lent it to exhibitions, because Picasso wanted it to go to Spain only when democracy returned. MoMA handed it over to the Spanish government in September 1981; it was first shown in the Casón del Buen Retiro and moved to the Reina Sofía in 1992.

stops.old: Photos of Guernica are not allowed.
stops.new: Photos are allowed without flash, tripod or selfie stick, unless a sign in the room says otherwise.

stops.old: Some 5,000 people were inside the town, around 2,000 of them troops and the rest civilians.
stops.new: Thousands of soldiers and civilians were inside the town.

stops.old: The fighting at Belchite cost the Nationalists about 2,000 dead and more than 2,400 captured.
stops.new: Losses were heavy on both sides, and many defenders were taken prisoner.

stops.set: Entry is by guided tour only (about 1½ hours, starting at the Arco de la Villa). Day tours run every day; night tours on Friday and Saturday focus more on local legends than on the battle. Buy tickets at the tourist office (C/ Becú 2, new town) or on belchite.es, and check prices and times there just before you go.
Casualty and prisoner totals for Belchite vary widely between sources, and depend on whether they count the town alone or the whole Zaragoza offensive, so this guide does not give a single figure.

stops.old: Three bombs hit the church and none exploded.
stops.new: Bombs fell on the church and the square beside it, and none exploded.

stops.set: The date, 3 August 1936, follows the standard study of the raid (J. Pujol Bertran, El bombardeo del templo del Pilar, 2023). Accounts differ on how many bombs fell, usually three or four.

Museo de los Mártires Claretianos, C/ Conde 4, Barbastro, about 50 km east of Huesca. Usually open Tuesday–Saturday 10:00–13:00 and 17:00–19:00 and Sunday 17:00–19:00; hours change, so check with the museum or the Barbastro tourist office before you go.

stops.old: The battalion lost about 150 killed and ceased to exist as a fighting unit.
stops.new: The battalion suffered very heavy losses and ceased to exist as a fighting unit.

stops.set: Published casualty totals differ, and many come from sources written on the requeté side, so no single figure is given here.
Codo is a short drive from Belchite and easily combined with Belchite and Quinto. The pin marks the village; ask locally for the memorial cross.

Museo de Bielsa 'José María Escalona', Plaza Mayor, Bielsa, with a section on the Bielsa Pocket and the exodus. Opening changes with the season, so check before you go or arrange a visit in advance. Bielsa is in the high Pyrenees near the tunnel to France; combine it with a walk in the valley.

stops.old: Today it houses an interpretation centre of the Espais de la Batalla de l'Ebre on the logistics of the battle.
stops.new: Today it houses the Centre d'Interpretació de les Guerres Carlines, which is also one of the Espais de la Batalla de l'Ebre, with panels on the battle and a commanding view over the town and the river crossings.

stops.set: The partly restored castle with its exhibition on the Carlist Wars and panels on the Battle of the Ebro, and views of the river crossing points below.
On the hill above the town centre. Opening is seasonal (summer afternoons; weekend mornings in winter), so check with the Móra d'Ebre tourist office.

stops.old: Between 1939 and 1952 about 1,700 people were shot here after court-martial, most of them buried in the Fossar de la Pedrera. The 'Fraternitat' monument by Miquel Navarro, erected in 1992, remembers them.
stops.new: Between 1939 and 1952, 1,686 people were shot here after court-martial, according to the figure the Generalitat uses for its new memorial. Most were buried in the Fossar de la Pedrera. The 'Fraternitat' monument by Miquel Navarro, erected in 1992, remembers them, and the Generalitat's memorial 'Bosc d'Empremtes' has one iron tube for each person shot.

stops.set: Counts differ because the registers and the areas counted differ: the Generalitat uses 1,686 (1939–52), the older plaque gives 1,734, and other studies give 1,717 executions in Barcelona for 1939–52. Executions here by the Republican side in 1936 are not well documented.
Barcelona Cathedral – the religious persecution of 1936

stops.old: A chapel in the cathedral precinct remembers the clergy of the diocese who were killed, some of whom have since been beatified.
stops.new: The cathedral is a place to reflect on this violence against the Church in Barcelona in 1936; some of the diocese's clergy killed then have since been beatified.

stops.set: The Gothic cathedral and its cloister on Carrer del Bisbe. Earlier versions of this guide mentioned a memorial chapel to the clergy killed in 1936; it has not been independently confirmed, so ask at the cathedral.

The shelter is visited with CIARGA (Centre d'Interpretació de l'Aviació Republicana i la Guerra Aèria), Parc de la Memòria, Santa Margarida i els Monjos. It usually opens at weekends and on holidays, 10:00–14:00, for a small fee; check with the town before you go.
MEDIUM

stops.old: On 5 February 1939 President Manuel Azaña walked across the frontier at the Coll de Lli into France. Lluís Companys and the Basque president José Antonio Aguirre crossed the same day.
stops.new: On 5 February 1939 President Manuel Azaña, Diego Martínez Barrio, Lluís Companys and the Basque president José Antonio Aguirre crossed the frontier into France on foot by the Coll de Lli.

stops.set: The pin marks the Monument a l'Exili at the entrance to La Vajol. From there the waymarked Ruta de l'Exili climbs about 6 km on forest tracks to the Coll de Lli on the French border; allow half a day on foot. The MUME exile museum in La Jonquera has route details.
San Marcial hermitage & the Battle of Irun

The San Marcial hermitage on its hilltop, a good viewpoint over the 1936 battlefield, Irun, Hendaye and the Bidasoa. The pin marks the hermitage, not a firing position; the fighting positions are not signposted.
Oviedo siege – the old town

stops.old: A memorial to the city's killed defenders is kept at the town hall.

stops.set: Central Oviedo, on foot. Earlier versions of this guide listed a memorial to the defenders inside the town hall; whether it is still on display has not been confirmed.
Casualty figures for the siege vary between sources and are not given here; civilian deaths are unclear.

stops.old: Roughly 1,000 men were killed on both sides.
stops.new: Both sides suffered heavy casualties; published totals vary.

stops.set: The 1958 Monumento a los Héroes del Simancas on the façade of the Colegio de la Inmaculada, Avenida Hermanos Felgueroso 25. It is a Francoist monument, shown here as a historical exhibit; the barracks building itself was later rebuilt.

Status in September 2026: the Asturian government ordered the monument's removal in May 2026, but the regional high court (TSJA) suspended that order in July while the case is decided. On 1 September 2026 the national government also listed it in the catalogue of symbols contrary to democratic memory, giving its owners six months to remove it. It may be gone or covered when you visit.
The pin marks Berango, not the centre's entrance: check the address and opening times with Uribe tourism before you go. Walks to the coastal bunkers around Sopela and Berango take 1–2 h.

stops.old: Morredondo and Cerro Cruz are each about an hour's walk from Viver.
stops.new: The pin marks Viver: Morredondo, Cerro Cruz and El Ragudo are separate sites around it. Morredondo and Cerro Cruz are each about an hour's walk from the town.

stops.set: Miranda de Ebro concentration camp (historic site)

The pin marks the old camp site, now among industrial plants, where a few remains survive; it does not mark every surviving structure. The interpretation centre, with a reconstructed barrack, is in the Centro Cívico Raimundo Porres, Avenida República Argentina 93, in town; check its opening hours with Miranda's tourist office.
Prisoner totals and deaths vary between sources. Figures such as 'up to 7,000 at a time' appear in some accounts but are not confirmed here.
Dec 1936–Nov 1939

stops.old: was turned into a concentration camp where most captured International Brigaders were held from 1938, alongside Spanish prisoners.
stops.new: was turned into a concentration camp in December 1936. From April 1938 it was the main camp for captured International Brigaders, held alongside Spanish prisoners, until it closed in November 1939.

stops.old: Cold, hunger and disease killed well over a hundred inmates, who were buried in the village cemetery. In the 2000s the association Pozo de Valdenoceda exhumed and identified many of them, making it one of the best-documented cases of prison mortality in Franco's Spain.
stops.new: Cold, hunger and disease killed 153 inmates between 1938 and 1943, and they were buried in the village cemetery. The victims' association counts 154, adding a man killed at Valdenoceda in 1936 before the prison opened. From 2007 the association exhumed 114 bodies and identified many of them, making it one of the best-documented cases of prison mortality in Franco's Spain.

stops.old: some 400 people are believed to have been shot and buried here.
stops.new: the official heritage declaration records 407 people buried here in three mass graves, killed between 10 September and 15 December 1936.

stops.set: Outside Lardero, a short drive from Logroño (the site is also called Barrigüelo); free, open air.
La Granja offensive – the battlefield above La Granja (Cabeza Grande, Matabueyes)

The pin marks La Granja, the starting point for the mountains above where the fighting took place; it is not a trench or strongpoint. Remains in the forest are not signposted, so keep to the paths. Avoid duplicating the Madrid-side Guadarrama stops.

context.old: Civilian allies included the fascist Falange, the Carlist Requetés of Navarre, monarchists and much of the Catholic right (CEDA).
context.new: Civilian supporters included the fascist Falange, the Carlist Requetés of Navarre, monarchists and people and networks of the Catholic right. CEDA itself was breaking up by 1936: its leader Gil Robles and others backed the conspirators, while many of its younger members moved into the Falange.

context.old: and the valley was renamed Cuelgamuros.
context.new: and the official name of the Valle de los Caídos was changed to Valle de Cuelgamuros, now a Place of Democratic Memory.

context.old: The Spanish Foreign Legion (Tercio), shock troops of the Army of Africa, co-founded by Millán-Astray and Franco.
context.new: The Spanish Foreign Legion (Tercio), created in 1920: shock troops of the Army of Africa. José Millán-Astray founded it; Franco was his second-in-command and led its 1st Bandera.
